The novel information or outcome from this project will include the prediction power of ASL CBF for early AD, CBF change rate when disease progresses or reverts, gender effects in AD and its progression, and a next-generation ASL MRI processing algorithm based on deep-machine learning (DL), and a DL-based AD prediction model. We will first confirm our previous ADNI ASL CBF findings using larger sample and updated methods (not available before). We will then check sensitivity of ASL CBF for tracking and predicting disease progression or cognitive declines. Gender effects on CBF in AD will be explicitly examined, which may reveal a clue for the higher prevalence of AD in females. We will revisit those studies using the DL-based ASL denoising algorithm. Pursuing those aims will help establishing ASL CBF as an AD biomarker and provide a versatile AD prediction model using ASL CBF as well as other valuable biomarkers provided in ADNI. Developing and sharing the DL ASL MRI denoising method will benefit not only AD research but also the various scientific projects based on ASL MRI. The feasibility of this innovative but clinically important project is ensured by our decades of experience and the substantial pilot investigations in each aspect of the study, including ASL MRI, AD ASL study, and machine learning.

projects.title: Exploring the Relationship Between Menopause and Cardiovascular Disease in Aging Women: A Longitudinal Analysis Using the NSHD Data
projects.summary:
Cardiovascular Disease (CVD) is the leading killer in ageing populations worldwide. With the development of technology and knowledge, various research indicates significantly there are gender differences, including sexual hormone levels, in vascular function. However, gender difference is often ignored when researchers or clinician doing their study. Notably, post-menopausal changes in estrogen levels are implicated in the increasing risk of CVD in women, yet the comprehensive effects of menopause on cardiovascular health are still unclear and clinically under-recognized (Robison et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2021).
Some studies imply that endothelial dysfunction plays a pivotal role in the development of Cardiovascular disease. Compared to men, endothelial dysfunction and the metabolic consequences it carries are more significant in women after menopause. The possible reason is that substances involved in vasodilation and vasoconstriction are synthesised and secreted by the endothelium of blood vessels, which can be mediated by estrogen levels. However, experiments need to be carried out to understand the protective function of estrogens and know more about their age and dose-dependent factors, thereby giving rise to effective treatment with fewer adverse effects. Many studies have demonstrated that some conceptive drugs can increase the risk of breast cancer and other reproductive system-related problems. (Gong et al., 2013)

Objective 
This project aims to investigate the association between various aspects of menopause (including age at onset, reproductive lifespan, hormone replacement therapy, menopausal symptoms, and pregnancy history) and the risk of n. We hypothesize that earlier onset of menopause increases the risk of CVD. Additionally, we aim to explore the relationship between menopause and cerebral small vessel disease, (MRI-imaging shape and location of white matter hyperintensity volume), contingent upon available time and resources.

Motivation and Hypothesis 
According to the improved understanding of the function of hormones, more attention is required for the prevention of cardiovascular disease in menopausal women. Therefore, this project aims to investigate how menopause (age, symptoms and treatment) is related to later-life cardiovascular disease (e.g.stroke, infarcts), which can provide further clarification into the associations between reproductive health and the rising risk of cardiovascular, taking into account measured hormone level post-menopausal at ages 53 and 60 (DHEAS, testosterone and pregnancy-related (number of children, fertility problems, pregnancy-related complications (pre
eclampsia, gestational diabetes) if there is enough time.

projects.title: The role of serum lipids profile during midlife and APOE gene in Alzheimer’s disease progression
projects.summary:
Brief Background: 

Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a neurodegenerative disorder characterized by progressive and irreversible decline in cognition. 1Recognizing that disease-modifying interventions have the greatest chance of success, the emphasis has shifted to controlling underlying risk factors such as diabetes mellitus2, hypertension3, smoking4, sleep disturbances5, and low educational attainment3. Moreover, it is reported that APOE4 affects the pathology of AD by multifaceted mechanisms, including abnormal lipid metabolism, inflammatory alterations, and impairment of astrocyte- and microglia-mediated Aβ clearance6,7.8 Dyslipidemia, mainly high level of low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-c), is thought to have vascular and neurotoxic effects and is implicated in the pathogenesis of AD9. However, the extent to which, and how, lipid profiles, such as low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-c), high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-c) and triglyceride (TG) in midlife, have a role in the development of AD, and its cognitive expression, is unknown. The concept of cognitive reserve suggests people can tolerate different levels of neuropathology, whereby those with less cognitive reserve can tolerate less pathology and this leads to earlier dementia onset. Dyslipidemia could either directly impact AD neuropathology, or contribute to cognitive reserve, lowering the threshold for cognitive impairment. 

 

Aim and Hypothesis: 

We aim to investigate how lipid profile during midlife (e.g. low levels of high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-c), along with high levels of triglyceride (TG)) are associated with AD-related pathology (PET/plasma amyloid proteins and MRI-hippocampal volume), cognition, and the interrelationship between amyloid and cognition (i.e. moderating the cognitive expression). We will explore how these associations vary by APOE-e4 carriers and sex. 

 

Aims: 

A: How are midlife lipids (age 53) associated with AD-biomarkers (age 70) (Amyloid/HV) 

Hypothesis: Having worse lipids (e.g. lower HDL) will be associated with greater amyloid burden and smaller hippocampal volume, indicative of AD. 

 

B: How are midlife lipids associated with cognitive function at age 70? 

Hypothesis: Having worse lipids (e.g. lower HDL) will be associated with poorer cognitive function. 

 

C: How does the relationship between lipids and AD biomarkers/cognition VARY (moderated)) By APOE-e4 or sex? 

Hypothesis: The relationship between worse lipids (e.g. lower HDL) and greater amyloid burden and smaller hippocampal volume, will be greater in APOE-e4 carriers vs non-carriers, and in men vs women. 

 

D: Does the relationship between AD-biomarkers And cognition VARY (moderated) by lipids? I.e. Do lipids change the tolerance threshold of amyloid affecting cognition, in line with cognitive reserve? 

Hypothesis: Having worse lipid profile in midlife (e.g. lower HDL) would lower tolerance of AD-burden when cognitive function is affected.

projects.title: The Relationship Between Health, Social Status, and Status-Seeking Personality
projects.summary: This project aims to investigate the interplay between health outcomes, socioeconomic status (SES), and Dominance personality. Social position significantly influences overall health through factors like income, education, housing, and healthcare access. Individuals of higher status have better access to resources promoting health, such as nutrition and social support. While research has focused on SES and health, less attention has been given to Dominance personality. Dominance traits, related to achieving higher social status, impact quality of life and health outcomes. Studies suggest a correlation between dominance traits and cardiovascular disease (CVD), with lower-ranking individuals experiencing more negative health effects. This project will explore how dominant personality traits influence health over time, using longitudinal data to study the relationship between dominance, social status, and health outcomes like cortisol levels, diabetes, and CVD. The study aims to clarify how dominance traits and social status impact health outcomes, potentially informing interventions to address health disparities.

projects.title: The effect of life-course physical activity on cardiac structure and function
projects.summary:
Introduction:
Cardiovascular disease (CVD) stands as the primary contributor to worldwide mortality, with its early roots traceable back to the initial ten years of life1. In adults, a noticeable connection exists between insufficient physical activity (PA) and an elevated likelihood of CVD onset2. Unequivocal evidence demonstrates that PA, particularly structured exercise training, has a significant positive impact on cardiovascular (CV) health3-5. However, the long-term effect of undertaking PA early in life on adult CV health, and specifically cardiac structure and function directly, is poorly understood. This project proposes to explore whether undertaking high volumes of PA in childhood and adolescence could cause positive cardiac ‘remodelling’ in adulthood and whether a similar relationship exists between mid-life PA and cardiac structure and function in elderly adults (>70 years old).
Strong evidence suggests that, although incidence CVD develops later in life, the processes involved in CVD development begin much earlier in life6-9. There are also likely to be long-term negative consequences of increasing rates of childhood obesity and sedentary behaviour10. Therefore, studying the early life behaviours related to adult CV health is an important research challenge. We propose to use data collected across the life-course from two longitudinal birth cohort studies currently running in the UK to explore this; the Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents and Children (ALSPAC)11 and the National Survey for Health and Disease (NSHD)12. ALSPAC is the only resource where cardiac function, measured using cutting-edge echocardiographic techniques at age 17 and 24, can be linked to antecedent objectively-measured PA exposure at ages 11, 13, 15, 17 and 24 years old. Traditional CV health outcomes, blood pressure (BP) and cholesterol from serum samples, have previously been linked to cardiac structure and function in ALSPAC13-16. NSHD is the world’s longest running
birth-cohort where participants, now age 77 years old, have recently undergone echocardiographic measurement of cardiac structure and function (along with other important CV health outcomes)17. As physical activity during the life course can affect cardiac function in elderly participants (75+ years old), the Medical Research Council National Survey of Health and Development (NSHD) offers a special chance to explore the factors throughout life that lead to cardiac issues within MyoFit46, which is the cardiac-focused part of the NSHD.
In addition to the important life-course analyses, this project will also explore the reproducibility and feasibility of the latest echocardiographic techniques, such as 3- dimension (3D) imaging during exercise, in order to establish if these methods could be suitable for characterising cardiac function in future research studies. We will compare echo-derived outcome measures with other imaging modalities, such as cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR).

projects.title: Implications of normalising hand grip strength and variation across ages in the UK
projects.summary:
Despite its utility, there is controversy around how best to interpret/use grip strength measures. A major challenge in clinical and research settings is its relationship with body size/composition. For example, taller individuals have greater grip strength due to the mechanical advantage of longer levers; heavier individuals (due to fat or muscle mass), particularly in young/mid-adulthood, have greater grip strength possibly due to the effect of greater loading. These relationships are acknowledged in the literature and are often used as justification to normalise grip strength (by adjustment or scaling), for measures of body size and/or composition: researchers include height as an adjustment in regression analyses for grip strength or scale grip strength for body mass or BMI. The heterogeneous approach to normalising grip strength evident in the literature, reflects the lack of a universally accepted normalising metric to remove the effect of body size/composition, with recent calls being made for this. However, few studies compare normalising grip strength by different body size and composition measures to determine the most appropriate measure(s) to be used. Additionally, similar to previous observations for body mass, when normalising grip strength, a further consideration is that the most appropriate normalising measure(s) to remove the effect of body size/composition could vary within the population. For example, the range and distribution of grip strength varies by age and sex. Body size and composition also vary by age and sex (differently to grip strength). Thus, it is feasible that the most appropriate normalising measure(s) to remove effects of body size/composition varies by age and sex.     
Another common measure of muscle function often collected at scale, is chair rise time. While both absolute grip strength and chair rise time depend on strength, they are poorly correlated as chair rise time captures other distinct aspects of function including balance and speed. Thus, researchers have begun to emphasize that these two measures of muscle function are not inter-changeable and they identify different people. Moreover, the impact of body size/composition on these functional measures are likely to vary because, for example, the weight-bearing load affecting grip strength and chair rise time is not the same. Importantly, there has recently been recognition that both absolute grip strength and chair rise time should be included in updated sarcopenia definitions. Thus, it is essential to understand of how normalising grip strength for body size/composition correlates with chair rise time.  
Given (i) the lack of consensus on how best to normalise grip strength to remove effects of body size/composition, (ii) the possibility that the normalising measure(s) could vary by age and sex and (iii) the uncertainty around how normalised grip strength correlates with chair rise time, we had three aims. First, we aim to identify the optimal body size/composition measure(s) that will normalize grip strength for differences in body size and composition among adults in midlife. Second, we aim to determine whether the optimal normalising measure(s) vary by age and sex and, third, how strongly the optimal normalised grip strength measures correlate with chair rise time.

projects.title: Investigating the distribution of and risk factors for plasma p-tau 217 in the National Survey of Health and Development
projects.summary: In Alzheimer’s disease (AD), two types of protein build up in the brain aberrantly. Recent advances in biochemistry now allow us to detect these protein build-ups using blood tests. The advent of blood tests that accurately detect the early development of AD will revolutionise research into the disease’s causes because we can now conduct large-scale studies without expensive, time-consuming or invasive alternate measures, such as neuroimaging or lumbar punctures. In this study, we will measure the most promising blood-based marker of AD to date, called p-tau 217, in blood samples collected from 952 NSHD participants at home visits when they were aged 69 years. We will use the information to study the determinants of AD, and how well the blood tests can predict risk of being clinically diagnosed with AD later in life.

projects.title: Multimodal longitudinal prediction of cerebrovascular disease
projects.summary:
1) Brief description of the context of the research including potential impact

Cerebral small vessel disease (CsVD) is a chronic intracranial vascular disease that affects the small vessels and blood blow in the brain. The disease is prevalent in 28% of people aged over 80 and may lead to brain damage and cognitive impairment. The progression of CsVD is multi-factorial and multi-pathological. One important type of lesion in CsVD are white matter hyperintensities (WMHs).

Multiple etiologies have been proposed to explain the progression in WMHs. The Rotterdam Scan Study has found age, blood pressure, current smoking and the presence of lacunar infarcts as predictors of WMH progression after three years' of follow-up. APOE4 is another a potential marker. Interestingly, baseline WMH lesion load was found to be associated with WMH progression in the LADIS study, indicating the condition's accelerating progression rate. While WMHs are positively associated with age, the histopathology of WMH is heterogeneous. A prospective study found WMH regression in 37% of minor ischemic stroke patients after 1 year. As the load and locations of WMHs could determine their clinical relevance, those factors should be incorporated in future research. This could be enabled by an automated regional-zonal WMH burden quantification method that was previously proposed to describe the spatial distribution of WMHs over 4 layers and 9 lobar zones.

2) Aims and Objectives

The aim of the four-year project is to predict the evolution of cerebral small vessel damage based on multiple types of data and support early intervention. It is hypothesised that such multimodal approaches could provide a better indication of how WMHs may progress over time. The baseline work should include MRI only, and other sources of information should be added incrementally. These sources include other neuroimaging modalities, cardiac imaging,
and clinical data. The deliverables should provide uncertainty estimation alongside the regional predictions, and should evaluate the impact of additional sources of information on the prediction performance.

As a logical first step, the first-year project will focus on the prediction of WMH load at the regional level. In addition to the regional WMH volumetric measures, experiments could include an ablation study of different markers from other sources (eg. blood pressure). The study should be rigorously conducted, and exploit both internal validation and external validation using an independent dataset if time permits. As the regional progression is provided, effort should be taken to identify patterns of how the lesions shrink, grow or remain stable at different locations of the brain. In terms of the modelling approaches, references could be made to studies on other brain or heart conditions.

1. Data: We have identified the publicly available Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative 3 (ADNI3) cohort as the primary dataset. The two-centred data was collected between 2017 and 2023 (data collection still ongoing). In addition to the MRI scans, demographic information (eg. age, sex), medical history (eg. blood pressure) and biomarkers (eg. APOE4) are also available.
2. Model input: While the 4-year project is aimed at making longitudinal predictions based on MRI scans in 3D, the input to the MRes project is primarily regional WMH volumes from the ADNI3 cohort. As mentioned above, demographics such as age and sex, medical history such as blood pressure could be added as part of the experiments.
3. Expected outcomes: The anticipated outcomes are longitudinal predictions of WMH volumes at different locations of the brain.

3) Novelty of Research Methodology

The student will develop image-based multi-modal longitudinal prediction of white matter hyperintensities where research is currently lacking. Further work will extend to other types of CsVD.

projects.title: Lifespan Dietary Trajectories and Gait Changes in Older Life
projects.summary:
As global demographics shift towards an older population, projected to make up 25% by 2050, understanding the keys to healthy aging is more critical than ever. Led by Dr. Tektonidis, our project focuses on how lifestyle factors such as diet, and potentially sleep and physical activity, influence aging, particularly through gait analysis—a proven indicator of health in older adults.

Project Goals:  
Develop a life-course dietary model to identify lifestyle patterns that promote healthy aging and enhance walking speed, an essential marker of health in older adults.

Key Activities:  
1. Data Analysis: Rigorous examination of the MRC NSHD/Insight46 cohort to identify how early and mid-life dietary patterns influence later-life health.
2. Model Development: Statistical modeling to explore the impact of diet, and possibly sleep and physical activity, on aging processes.
3. Collaboration and Dissemination: Work with UCL to extend research findings through high-impact publications and academic forums, aiming to inform public health strategies.

Impact:  
This project aims to pinpoint non-clinical lifestyle adjustments that can significantly improve public health outcomes for the aging population, focusing on diet as a pivotal factor.

Timeline:  
Initiate detailed data management and analysis from May 2024, with findings to be developed and shared by July 2024 onwards.
Our research will provide actionable insights that support maintaining health and functionality into later life, directly impacting clinical practices and public health recommendations.

projects.title: Genetic effects of human DNA methylation levels
projects.summary: Our original project aimed to profile and explore DNA methylation levels across UK cohorts, to assess changes with age and age-related phenotypes. As part of this work, we also explored evidence for genetic influence on the DNA methylome, resulting in a recent publication (Villicana et al. 2023. Genome Biology).  We now wish to extend this component of the workflow, focussing on identifying genetic influences on the human DNA methylome within larger collaborative research efforts.

projects.title: Investigating the mechanisms linking psychiatric disorders with subsequent cognitive decline and dementia
projects.summary:
Previous research suggests that psychiatric symptoms and disorders are associated with higher risk of cognitive decline and dementia. However, temporality and causality of these relationships remains unclear, and little is known about possible underlying mechanisms. 
     For instance, psychiatric disorders, including depression and anxiety, have been linked with poor cardiometabolic health, and related health behaviours including smoking, higher alcohol consumption, and low levels of physical activity.. Poor cardiometabolic health has, in turn, been identified as risk factors for dementia, and could therefore be important pathways in explaining the links between mental health, cognition and dementia. Further, accumulating evidence implicates systemic inflammation in the pathophysiology of dementia and psychiatric disorders.
     Despite the plausibility of these potential pathways, few studies have directly tested the mechanisms underlying these relationships. The limited research in this area highlights the need for further longitudinal research investigating longitudinal relationships between psychiatric symptoms, cognitive trajectories and dementia in large studies with long follow-up periods. In particular, further research is needed to investigate potential mechanisms underlying these relationships, including cardiovascular health, health behaviours, inflammation and HPA axis dysfunction.
     To address these gaps in knowledge, first, we aim to investigate longitudinal relationships between psychiatric symptoms, subsequent cognitive trajectories and, where possible, dementia risk in a cross-cohort study involving NSHD, Whitehall II, the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing, and the Swedish Study on Aging and Care in Kungsholmen. We will also investigate potential mediators of relationships between psychiatric symptoms, cognition and dementia, including health behaviours, cardiovascular health, inflammatory biomarkers and cortisol. Gaining insight into underlying mechanisms could have important implications for dementia prevention and early detection.

projects.title: Analysing the imaging, blood and cognitive variables influencing premotor signs in the Insight 64 cohort
projects.summary: Brain disorders like Parkinson and Alzheimer’s disease tend to affect elderly people more than younger people. Beyond ageing, however, it is not clear what other factors – such as blood results and the appearance of the brain on scans – contribute to the risk of developing such brain disorders. This project is aimed at analysing data gathered from one of the oldest groups of British people who have been followed since their birth in England, Scotland and Wales during one week in March 1946. Specifically, I will analyse what factors predict problems in movement typically seen in Parkinson disease. These findings are important as they will inform us on how to better predict and diagnose conditions such as Parkinson disease, and suggest strategies to reduce the risk of developing such conditions.

projects.title: Glucose Variability and Cognitive Performance in older adults: Insights from Continuous Glucose Monitoring
projects.summary:
With an increasingly ageing population, cognitive health is an important research topic. Dementia and Diabetes are two of the most pronounced health conditions affecting millions of people worldwide, with huge individual and societal implications. Current research indicates an interplay between glucose dysregulation and cognitive performance (Xia et al., 2020). However, it is not yet understood how. 
Advancements in CGM can identify blood glucose at a more precise level and more frequently, to received real time metrics (Matabuena et al., 2023). 
To further investigate into the relationship between blood glucose and cognition in older age, we will explore how Continuous Glucose Monitors metrics from Insight 46 participants, a neuroscience sub-study of the MRC National Survey of Health and Development, is linked with their cognitive function from cognitive assessments.

projects.title: Epigenetic contributions to white matter changes in dementia
projects.summary: The brain is composed of two types of tissue: grey matter, and white matter. The latter makes up half of the human brain and provides essential links between several brain areas, including those needed for movement and memory. Recent studies looking at brain images have shown that white matter changes have strong implications in Alzheimer’s disease (AD). However, it is not known how, why, and when such changes occur. A process called DNA methylation controls the amount of proteins produced and may dictate how cells function and survive. DNA methylation can be influenced by many factors, including lifestyle, and can potentially be corrected therapeutically. Although the importance of DNA methylation in AD grey matter is recognised, DNA methylation has never been studied in AD white matter, and thus our understanding is limited. With this project, through collaboration with researchers from around the world, we will use data from over 1900 individuals, including blood DNA methylation data and brain images as well as clinical and lifestyle data. This project aims to link DNA methylation from brain and blood to white matter damage seen in brain images, and to clinical and lifestyle data. This will produce new biomarkers to help predict AD risk and measure disease progression.

projects.title: Associations Between Socioeconomic Status and Mental Health Mediated by Smoking, Physical Activity, and Diet in a Longitudinal Cohort
projects.summary: This project aims to explore how socioeconomic status (SES) influences anxiety and depression through health behaviors such as smoking, physical activity, and diet. Previous studies have shown that individuals with lower SES are more likely to engage in smoking, have less physical activity, and maintain poorer diets, and all these factors are strongly linked to higher rates of anxiety and depression. This project plans to analyze how these behaviors mediate the relationship between SES and anxiety and depression by using structural equation modeling. Participants are drawn from the 1946 British national birth cohort of the MRC National Survey of Health and Development, using variables related to social class, income, occupation, smoking, physical activity, diet, and mental health. The expected results should confirm that modifying health behaviors, especially in lower SES groups, can effectively reduce issues of anxiety and depression. These findings will provide evidence for designing public health initiatives to improve mental health across different SES groups.

projects.title: Level and Change in perceived control in the lifespan: Findings From a British Birth Cohort Study
projects.summary: Longitudinal data spanning from childhood to adulthood and later life will be employed to track the developmental trajectory of perceived control. This research aims to inform policy-making and interventions aimed at promoting individual well-being and societal health.

projects.title: The First Baby Boomers: Ten stories of education and everyday life in postwar Britain
projects.summary: This is a project for a popular history book called 'The First Baby Boomers: Ten stories of education and everyday life in postwar Britain'. The book will use qualitative and quantitative study member data from the NSHD, as well as study metadata and wider contextual information and secondary literature, to write a history of postwar Britain through the lives of ten ordinary people, with a special focus on their educational journeys and trajectories. The book will be published in 2026 to coincide with the 80th birthday of the study members and the NSHD.

projects.title: Swarm Learning-Based PRS
projects.summary: To facilitate better integration of available datasets within DPUK platform while preserving the privacy of genetic data we propose to implement Swarm Learning (SL) - a novel approach for harnessing distributed genetic data in application to dementia research. By exploring Swarm learning approaches within the DPUK, this project aims to understand the feasibility of privacy-preserving research methodologies and data and further pave the way for potential future collaborations within other sites or platforms where data cannot be directly shared.

projects.title: Investigating the role of common pathogens in heart, brain and ageing health
projects.summary: Many common infectious agents may play a role in the deterioration of cardiovascular, neurological or other physiological processes as individuals age. For example, nine herpesviruses commonly infect humans, and establish lifelong latency - mounting repeated immunological challenges during periods of reactivation. The aim of this research is to investigate whether exposure to individual pathogens, or many together in combination, are related to markers of cardiovascular, neurological, and overall health in older individuals. To do so, we will use multiplex serology technology to assay antibodies against at least 13 common pathogens in 1815 plasma samples biobanked from the 60-64 year follow-up of the NSHD. These data will allow us to study cross-sectional and prospective associations of individual serological markers of infections and overall pathogen burden with various cardiovascular, neurovascular, neurodegenerative and gerontological outcomes collected at the 60-64 year follow-up and later data collections (Insight 46 and MyoFit46).

projects.title: MyoFit46
projects.summary:
For a long time, higher priority was given to heart research in younger people over that in older people. As a result, there is a lack of knowledge about the way the heart functions in older people. This is now an urgent problem because, thanks to modern medicine, there will soon be over 500 million people on earth aged 75 or older.
We want to understand how the environment and events during infancy, childhood and adulthood, including avoidable childhood infections and lifestyle, affect the wellbeing of our hearts as we grow older. We propose to investigate the hearts of individuals in the world's longest running research population (Britain’s 1946 population study) using the best and safest heart imaging camera available (MRI). We anticipate that cleaner air, vaccination and healthier lifestyles all contribute to keeping the heart healthier for longer. 
Our research will help to preserve heart health and help doctors take better care of the hearts of older persons.

projects.title: Developing blood based biomarkers to detect preclinical Alzheimer's disease and predict progression

projects.title: A lifetime of stammering: feasibility and scoping
projects.summary: Life stressors such as the stigma that people who stammer can experience make people more likely to develop mental health problems such as anxiety and depression. This project will use existing longitudinal cohort datasets to look back retrospectively on important outcomes over a lifetime of stammering. While these studies are not specifically about stammering the cohorts are large and a number of the people who have provided data over the course of their lives will have stammered. This project will test whether cohort members who stammer were more likely to develop mental health problems such as depression over their lifespan.

projects.title: Associations between lifelong exposure to anticholinergic medication, later life cognition and amyloid burden.
projects.summary: The project will look into lifelong exposure to anticholinergic medications, and their associations with later life cognitive outcomes. A key outcome studied will be the amyloid burden seen on neuroimaging from the Insight46 substudy; an important proponent of Alzheimer's dementia risk.

projects.title: Investigating the connection between proteomic age and mortality
projects.summary:
Just as different people show different outward signs of ageing, so our bodies also age at different speeds throughout adulthood (biological ageing). Recent scientific advances suggest that this biological age can be estimated from changes linked to the body’s proteins (proteomics). There is emerging evidence that people with more rapid biological ageing are at higher risk of developing chronic diseases and dying in later life. 

My research will test this theory in hundreds of people who were born throughout the UK in the same week in 1946, and are therefore all the same age. These people have been tracked by researchers since their birth and have detailed measurement of disease and health status. I will examine whether the people with the fastest biological proteomic ageing are most likely to develop chronic diseases and die earlier in later life.

projects.title: Home-based Sleep and Physiological Monitoring (InSleep46)
projects.summary: The aim of this project is to collect several health-related measurements using an electronic internet-enabled sleep mat installed under participants' mattresses in their home. This electronic “smart” device can connect via Wi-Fi to a smartphone or tablet device. The device uses pressure sensors to detect information regarding movement, sleep quality, heart rate and breathing. The project hopes to identify sleep patterns that can predict increased risk of developing dementia.

projects.title: Insight 46 Sleep
projects.summary:
Sleep is an essential requirement of all animal life, including humans, who spend around a third of their life asleep. We do not understand why humans need to sleep, however it is becoming clear that sleep is linked to cognition (brain functions such as thinking and memory). Even short periods of sleep deprivation result in worse cognitive function and signs of damage to the brain. Evidence is emerging that disrupted sleep may be part of the cause of Alzheimer's disease.

We do not know how or when abnormal sleep patterns emerge, how they change over time, or how they relate to cognition in the long term. It is unclear if disturbed sleep patterns are early signs of disease, or if they precede and cause neurodegenerative diseases. To answer these questions we must analyse sleep in detail.

We plan to examine sleep in relation to cognition and neurodegeneration in the NSHD. Unpicking these relationships is essential to improving our understand neurodegenerative diseases, and has important implications for their diagnosis and treatment.

projects.title: The arrhythmogenic potential of midwall septal fibrosis in non-ischaemic dilated cardiomyopathy – a combined CMR/ECGI investigative study
projects.summary:
Scarring of the heart muscle detected by magnetic resonance is associated with higher risk of life threatening arrhythmias (very fast and abnormal beating of the heart) in patients with primary dilated and/or arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathies (diseases of the heart muscle in the absence of a prior heart attack or inflammatory condition). The mechanisms to explain this association remain poorly understood. Also, dilated and/or arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathies are associated with the risk of death and adverse cardiac events such as heart failure. 
We will use a special device called ECGi to record the electrical activity of the heart from the chest surface, and we will combine the recordings with cardiac magnetic resonance findings.
The aim is to investigate the potential of cardiac scar to cause arrhythmias, as well as its capacity to predict cardiac deaths and/or other adverse cardiac events in patients with primary dilated and/or arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathies .

projects.title: Is fat mass a better predictor than body mass index of the long-term health consequences of childhood obesity?
projects.summary:
Background:
Historically, due to the absence of accurate and practical methods to assess the amount of fat within an individual, body mass index (BMI), a weight-based proxy, has been used in its place. Though simple to calculate, BMI provides inaccurate assessment of childhood body fat and identification of children suffering with obesity. Accurate and practical methods to assess body fat itself are now available and may be more strongly related to future disease risks than BMI, and will allow for more accurate identification of children at higher risk of long-term diseases.

The Plan:
I will apply a new method for accurately assessing childhood body fat within childhood studies from the UK, Europe, America, and India in which information on later chronic disease development is available for these children in adulthood. I will: (i) examine the association between childhood body fat and future disease risk several decades later, (ii) investigate whether body fat allows us to identify children at risk of future disease more accurately than BMI, and (iii) define childhood fat mass thresholds which are based on the risk of an individual developing chronic disease later in life. 

Why is this important? 
Childhood obesity is common and increasing, representing a major public health challenge worldwide. Given the limitations of BMI in childhood, and the availability of accurate methods to assess childhood fat mass, it is important to assess whether childhood fat mass is a more accurate marker of future health risk than BMI. These investigations will offer the possibility for improving the assessment of childhood body fat both in individual children and in populations, shifting the focus back on to fat mass assessment and it’s subsequent consequences on health risks.
projects.institution: Center for Clinical Research and Prevention (Copenhagen) and Dasman Diabetes Institute (Kuwait)

projects.title: Longitudinal trajectories of self-reported subjective cognitive decline in relation to objective cognitive performance, in a population-based cohort
projects.summary: Subjective cognitive decline (SCD) is the self-reported worsening of cognitive abilities despite seemingly performing normally on objective cognitive tests. Evidence suggests that self-reported concerns are one of the earliest symptoms of Alzheimer’s Disease (AD) and therefore may represent subtle cognitive decline before impairment can be detected on standard cognitive tests. However, this exact nature of the relationship between self-report decline and performance on objective cognitive tests is unclear. This project aims to understanding the relationship between SCD and AD by exploring the longitudinal association between SCD, cognition and brain health.

projects.title: Genetic and Socioeconomic Influences on Cognitive Ability Across Generations
projects.summary:
This project aims to understand how genetic predispositions and socioeconomic circumstances interact to shape cognitive abilities across generations. Using data from three major British birth cohorts—the 1946 National Survey of Health and Development, the 1958 National Child Development Study, and the 1970 British Cohort Study—this research will explore how a person’s genetic predisposition for certain cognitive traits combines with their social and economic environments throughout their life, and how these interactions may have changed over time.

The study focuses on how socioeconomic factors, such as parents' occupation and education, as well as an individual's own career and educational achievements, interact with genetic predispositions to impact cognitive abilities. It examines both the independent effects of these factors and how they work together in various contexts.

By identifying key points where targeted interventions could make a difference, this project seeks to inform policies and strategies aimed at reducing socioeconomic inequalities in cognitive health and promoting healthy cognitive ageing across the life course

projects.title: Investigating the role of common pathogens in heart, brain and ageing health
projects.summary: Individuals in the UK are exposed to many germs that cause infections. These are often benign or have only minor health consequences in childhood and early adulthood, but may play a more insidious role in ill health as people age and their immune systems weaken. In particular, researchers are concerned that common viruses and bacteria may cause harm to the heart and brain tissues over long periods of time through a variety of mechanisms. However, these links are not concrete, and require further investigation. In this study, we will use recently developed blood tests to identify whether members of the NHSD had been exposed to at least 13 common infectious agents by their early 60s, and use this information to investigate whether these infections might (individually or in combination) be having detrimental effects on the heart, brain and overall health of individuals as they age.

projects.title: Predictors of successful cognitive aging in European superagers (90+) a cross-platform investigation of research and real-world evidence
projects.summary:
The aim of this collaborative European cross-platform project to construct a database of 85-90 + year olds to facilitate the understanding of successful ageing.
 This database will enable researchers to conduct multi-level statistical analyses which will enhance understanding about which variables are associated with
 higher levels of cognition in this older population and also those variables associated with the absence of dementia. Moreover, in an epidemiological context,
 this project has a valuable opportunity to play a role in contributing towards understanding the target audience for clinical trials, therapeutic interventions and
 long term monitoring and education.
 The outcome of the creation of this database therefore has extensive opportunities in creating prediction models not only in epidemiological dementia-related
 research but also for epidemiological health-related research across the entire lifespan.

projects.title: Visual function in later life and its association with Alzheimer’s disease biomarkers and cognition
projects.summary: Dementia is associated with increased prevalence of visual impairment. The mechanisms underlying this association are unclear but several possibilities have been proposed. First, it is known that diseases which cause dementia can affect the areas in the brain which are responsible for vision. Second, dementia and visual impairment have many shared risk factors including older age, diabetes and high blood pressure. Finally, the presence of visual impairment itself may make individuals more susceptible to developing dementia. To investigate this further, this project will use data from the Insight 46 neuroimaging sub-study of the NSHD to examine associations between basic visual function parameters, health-related risk factors, brain imaging measures and cognitive function in later life.

projects.title: International evaluation of modifiable social determinants of health on COVID-related mental health outcomes
projects.summary:
The COVID-19 pandemic has brought numerous challenges for global mental health, with diverse studies documenting worsening trends in psychiatric symptoms. Individuals with pre-existing mental health conditions have experienced increased rates of psychiatric disorders and mortality. The substantial mental health burden associated with the pandemic has been thought to be driven in large part by the confluence of factors related to social determinants of health (SDoH). These have likely included direct effects of public health measures (e.g., lockdowns and social distancing) and indirect effects (e.g., unemployment and interruptions in access to healthcare). Importantly, these impacts have been unevenly distributed, exacerbating national and global health disparities. Despite the volume of research on the 
mental health impact of the pandemic, several gaps exist in our understanding of the drivers of risk and resilience, including: 1) many studies have been cross-sectional, limiting inferences about trajectories of risk; 2) relatively limited attention to the interplay between social distancing interventions and risk factors that interact to influence the mental health burden; 3) many studies have lacked global representation, limiting the ability to make informative comparisons across contexts. 

Addressing these gaps is thus of immense public benefit. We aim to conduct a global evaluation of pandemic-related mental health outcomes, using individual-level longitudinal data harmonized across cohorts. We propose to leverage and expand this unique asset to fill critical knowledge gaps around the impact of policy, psychological, and social factors on mental health in the pandemic. This application will 
analyze modifiable targets uniquely or robustly implicated in the pandemic and relevant to new and worsening mental illness and, in particular, examine the impact of pandemic-related changes in social determinants of health.

projects.title: Examining the relationships between long-term health, multimorbidity and economic outcomes
projects.summary: Poor health is a significant driver of negative economic outcomes, affecting individuals' ability to work and participate in the labour market. Poor health can reduce productivity, increase absenteeism, and may force early retirement, exacerbating economic inequalities. The interplay between health and economic outcomes is particularly critical for individuals with multiple chronic conditions (multimorbidity), which can further reduce their participation in the workforce. Here we use the NSHD cohort to examine the relationships between health and subsequent economic outcomes including economic inactivity due to ill health, switching from full-time to part-time work, uptake of benefits and subjective opinions towards their financial situation. This work will examine the impact of a range of short- and long-term health conditions individually as well as cumulative exposures such as multimorbidity, examining the potential mediation by a range of modifiable factors.

projects.title: Head injury and hearing loss - predictors of longitudinal change in Insight 46
projects.summary:
Preventing dementia is one of the most important health challenges of the 21st century. One potential approach of preventing dementia that has been proposed is to aim to improve brain health by addressing a number of factors that are felt to increase risk of subsequent dementia. Two examples of such factors include hearing loss and head injury. However, the precise nature of the relationship between hearing loss/head injury and brain health and how this could increase the chances of someone developing dementia is unclear. The aim of this project would be to investigate whether hearing ability (measured using a series of tests of hearing), or head injury, lead to changes in detailed measurements of brain structure (using advanced techniques that analyse brain scans) or changes in performance on detailed tests of memory and thinking in older adults.

This research would aim to improve understanding of how hearing loss and head injury may lead to dementia, with the hope that his will guide further research and inform strategies for preventing dementia in the future.

projects.title: Investigating relationships between cardiovascular risk factors, AD biomarkers, WM integrity and cognition
projects.summary: Determining if cardiovascular health and AD-related pathology is related to decline in white matter microstructure, and if this decline is related to cognitive performance

projects.title: Understanding the biological basis of Gompertzian ageing in human populations
projects.summary:
In many animal species, mortality rates rise exponentially with increasing age. This so-called “demographic ageing” is widely believed to reflect biological ageing: the physiological and functional declines in health at older ages that lead eventually to death. Accordingly, the mathematical parameters of the exponential function (Gompertz function) used to model demographic ageing have common biological interpretations. Most commonly, the scale of exponential increase is thought to reflect ageing-independent mortality risks, while the rate of exponential increase is thought to reflect the rate of ageing. However, these relationships between demographic and biological ageing are conjectural and untested.

Recent animal model data suggest that these traditional biological interpretations of Gompertzian ageing are largely incorrect. Here, we aim to similarly investigate the biological basis of Gompertzian ageing in human populations.

projects.title: Exploring the Link Between Childhood Socioeconomic Status and Late-Life Cognition: Mediating Roles of Midlife BMI and Blood Pressure
projects.summary:
Dementia, a condition characterized by cognitive decline, has experienced a shocking surge in recent decades and is expected to triple in the coming years. While there is no current cure, research suggests that addressing risk factors such as obesity and high blood pressure - particularly in the midlife period - may reduce the risk of developing dementia in later life.

Early exposure to adverse socioeconomic status (SES) in childhood has been linked a wide-range of long-lasting adverse health outcomes in later life, including obesity, high blood pressure, and cognitive decline and dementia.

This research aims to explore the extent by which midlife risk factors such as blood pressure and BMI may explain known links between childhood SES and cognitive health in late-life. The findings will help identify modifiable risk factors, providing insights into potential strategies to prevent dementia and promote healthy aging.

projects.title: Relationships between radiological reads and automatically extracted biomarkers of cerebral small vessel disease (CSVD).
projects.summary:
Radiologists often perform radiological reads when looking at brain scans. This involves manually interpreting the scans and making visual assessments on different findings (biomarkers) that could indicate the presence of cerebral small vessel disease (CSVD.) This process is often time-consuming and could be affected by subjectivity, as assessments are based on individual radiologists’ judgment. Recently, techniques employing artificial intelligence (AI) -based algorithms, have been developed to provide automated methods of identifying these biomarkers from brain scans. These methods offer a standardised approach to accurately quantifying CSVD biomarkers. Given the variability in traditional radiological assessment, this project aims to compare radiological reads to these automated methods of biomarker extraction. Of the different CSVD biomarkers that exist, white matter hyperintensities (WMH) will be focused on specifically. Currently, information about WMH measurements is in the form of brief comments written by the radiologists. During this project, these comments will be encoded into numerical values, allowing comparison with the automatically extracted data. 

Within healthcare, inconsistencies in identifying and reporting CSVD biomarkers contribute to delays in diagnosing patients and initiating appropriate management. The findings of this project may help to build on recent improvements to diagnostic guidelines. They may also assist in highlighting opportunities for computer-aided tools to be used alongside traditional radiologist judgement, to enhance detection and diagnosis of the disease.

projects.title: Patterns of life course physical activity and CVD outcomes
projects.summary: Physical activity is linked with reduction of major heart problems, but we still don’t fully understand how exercise at different stages of life affects heart health and overall lifespan. Our study aims to explore the long-term impact of physical activity on heart disease, heart attacks, and heart failure. We also seek to answer key questions like how much exercise is needed to significantly lower heart disease risk, when in life exercise is most effective, and whether adults who were previously inactive can still benefit.

projects.title: Pollution and cerebrovascular burden
projects.summary: This project will look at the long term effects of pollution exposure and blood supply to the brain. This will be done by examining lifelong and childhood pollution exposure in a dataset of 5362 people born in 1946 and examining late life brain MRi scans which will show us areas and volumes of the brain with poorer blood supply. Poor cerebral blood supply is associated with dementia, stroke and increased risk of death therefore this project is important to determine modifiable risk factors for brain and heart disease and we hypothesise that there is a link between childhood pollution exposure and poor brain blood supply.

projects.title: Investigating the association between smoking and later-life patterns of white matter hyperintensities
projects.summary:
White matter hyperintensities (WMH), also called leukoaraiosis, are bright spots that appear on brain scans (MRI FLAIR) and are linked to blood vessel problems in the brain. These spots can signal issues like a leaky blood-brain barrier, damage to nerve fibers, and loss of the protective myelin coating around nerves. WMHs are connected to cognitive problems and significantly increase the risks of stroke and dementia. Smoking plays a big role in the development of WMH by harming blood vessels and brain tissue. It causes issues like poor blood flow to the brain, inflammation, and oxidative stress, all of which can lead to nerve damage and the formation of these white matter lesions. 
This study looks at how smoking affects WMH patterns later in life, focusing on where they occur in the brain and their shape. It uses data from the National Survey of Health and Development (NSHD) cohort, including a group called Insight 46. The study will examine smoking history and how much people smoked up to age 63. It will also analyse data to measure the size, location, and shape of WMHs. 
To study the connection between smoking and WMH, we will use a statistical method called regression analysis to help us see how WMH volume changes with smoking habits while accounting for factors like age, socioeconomic status, and gender. The brain will also be divided into four layers (from the deepest to the surface) to see how smoking affects WMH in different parts of the brain. The goal is to understand whether smoking is linked to WMH, how much WMH increases with more smoking, and whether these changes are significant.

projects.title: Heart rate trajectories over the lifecourse in NSHD and their relation to outcomes
projects.summary: This study aims to model heart trait trajectories ,assessing how heart rate changes, throughout the life course of participants born in 1946. These participants had physical measurements such as heart rate and blood pressure taken from childhood and time allowing, the study will look at the association between resting heart rate and adverse outcomes such as atrial fibrillation and stroke.

projects.title: Blood Pressure Trajectories over the Lifecourse in NSHD and Their Relation to Cardiovascular Disease among Adults
projects.summary: This study aims to explore the blood pressure trajectories of the same group of individuals across the lifecourse and establish an understanding of the correlation between their BP profiles and the onset and progression of cardiovascular diseases, offering valuable insight into the potential between BP fluctuations and cardiovascular health outcomes in adulthood, hence benefit the future development of clinical strategies to relieve disease burden.

projects.title: Prediction of Events from Wearables
projects.summary:
Technological advancement in wearable and mobile-health devices provides new opportunities for assessing health and risk at scale, using data collected in the community during free-living activities. Most of consumer-grade wearable devices including smart watches, rings etc. continuously track heart rate and physical activity. Despite a growing interest in using wearable technology for mobile health applications, to the extent of our knowledge there is currently no data on the use of wearable-derived heart rate data to predict long-term clinical outcomes in the general population. 
The aim of this study is to address this knowledge gap by using data collected in participants aged 60-64 from the MRC National Survey of Health and Development (NSHD) who between 2006 and 2010 were given a wearable device that measured heart rate and physical activity continuously for 7 days. 
This study will use machine learning and artificial intelligence models to predict major adverse clinical events based on heart rate and physical activity trajectories.

projects.title: Amyloid DuAl-biomarker PeT for DEmEntia diAgnosis and subTyping (ADAPT DEfEAT)
projects.summary: The aim of this project is to generate dual-biomarker PET data, producing estimates of both relative blood flow and amyloid deposition from the dynamic amyloid data. Disease progression modelling will be applied to the dual biomarkers for improved disease subtype and staging.

projects.title: Investigating relationships between inflammatory biomarkers and white matter hyperintensities
projects.summary:
Lay Summary: White Matter Changes in the Brain and Inflammation

This research project aims to understand how inflammation in the body might be connected to certain changes in the brain that appear as bright spots on brain scans (called white matter hyperintensities or WMH). Understanding these relationships could help us better understand how inflammation contributes to brain changes as we age. This might eventually lead to new approaches for preventing or treating age-related brain conditions.

projects.title: Understanding the genetic architecture of grip strength in middle age and older adults
projects.summary: This project will explore the genetic factors that influence grip strength, which is often used as a measure of overall muscle strength and is an important sign of physical health. Grip strength is closely linked to many different health outcomes. We will conduct a genomewide association study of grip within UK Biobank and seek to replicate findings within the UK birth cohorts (NSHD, 1958BC and BCS70). Importantly, we will not adjust for measures of body size such as BMI, weight or height in our analysis. This will help us better understand the complex relationship between body size and grip strength, and how both are connected to other health factors.

projects.title: Harmonising across the British birth cohorts
projects.summary: Our aim is to enhance data from five British birth cohorts through retrospective harmonisation of 1) fertility data and 2) physical health variables, thereby enabling more cross-cohort research using these rich datasets. The five cohort studies included are: the Millennium Cohort Study (MCS, 2000-02), Next Steps (1989-90), the 1970 British Cohort Study (BCS70), the 1958 National Child Development Study (NCDS), and the 1946 MRC National Survey of Health and Development (NSHD). We will deposit these data on the UKDS.

projects.title: Personalised brain imaging for Alzheimer's research and trials using neuroanatomical normative modelling: going beyond the average patient
projects.summary:
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans have shown how Alzheimer’s disease affects the brain on average; however, Alzheimer’s patients are all different, so understanding the ‘average patient’ has limited clinical use. Here, we will use a new way to measure an individual patient’s brain health by comparing their brain scans to a separate set of scans from almost 60,000 healthy people. This approach, called normative modelling, is commonly used for height and weight growth charts for children. Here, we will apply this idea to separate brain areas, to determine whether someone’s brain looks bigger or smaller than expected for their age and sex. Having a smaller than expected brain area is likely due to brain ‘atrophy’, the loss of brain cells. Brain atrophy is a key factor that drives the symptoms seen in people with Alzheimer’s.
Our project will collate an additional 12,000 brain scans taken from several ageing and dementia studies into a database, which will be actively managed throughout the project. Then using this database, we plan to show that ‘brain normative modelling’ can 1) track early disease changes in a person’s brain before Alzheimer’s symptoms start, 2) be applied to people from underrepresented demographics (e.g., based on ethnicity), 3) improve how clinical trials of potential Alzheimer’s treatments work, by comparing our method to previous ways of analysing brain scans.
By focusing on how everyone’s brain is unique, rather than assuming one-size-fits-all, our project will show how brain MRI can be used for personalised medicine for people with Alzheimer’s.

projects.title: The predictive value of ptau-217 at age 70
projects.summary: This project focuses on a blood test called ptau-217 that measures the levels of phosphorylated tau protein in plasma. We are investigating what the results of this test at age 70 mean for subsequent brain health over the next 8 years,  looking at measures from brain scans, cognitive tests and dementia diagnosis from health records. We hope that this will be an important contribution to the field at a time when population screening for ptau-217 is being considered, and such screening is already being carried out to determine eligibility for clinical trials.

projects.title: Quantifying severity of CSVD
projects.summary: Quantifying the severity of Cerebral Small Vessel Disease

projects.title: Long Covid-19 related sleep impairments: A new factor in the progression from preclinical Alzheimer's Disease to dementia?
projects.summary:
Five years after Covid-19, we are just beginning to see its long-term consequences, especially for those at risk of or suffering from Alzheimer’s disease (AD). Many people continued to struggle beyond the health and economic impacts. They faced lasting symptoms that hurt their quality of life through a condition called Long Covid-19
(LC19). Disrupted sleep is very common in LC19, affecting about 1 in 3 individuals. Similar changes in sleep appear in preclinical AD, linked to early brain changes and Amyloid buildup. Poor sleep is also a key factor in AD progression. Yet, no study has looked at how sleep problems might worsen decline in people with preclinical AD who suffered from LC19. We will analyse sleep patterns using activity data from a British study on early AD. We will group participants by their Amyloid-β burden status and LC19 diagnosis to create profiles of sleep issues. After validation, changes in key indicators of AD progression will be compared between groups: blood markers levels, cognitive function, and brain structure decline. We expect to see worse sleep and faster disease progression in people with preclinical AD who also had LC19. Our results will lay the groundwork for future studies in different populations. They will provide new insights into the link between sleep and AD, especially with a potential new risk factor: LC19. We will share our findings with communities looking to raise awareness about good sleep hygiene habits and how this can make a difference for people affected by AD and LC19.

projects.title: Genetic Modifiers of TTR Amyloidosis
projects.summary:
Hereditary transthyretin (hATTR) amyloidosis is a rare genetic systemic disease caused by mutations in the transthyretin (TTR) gene. Mutant TTR protein tends to accumulate across different tissues and organs, especially peripheral nerves and the heart. This is a progressive, disabling, and life-threatening condition with a mean survival of 4.7 years from diagnosis if left untreated. Wild-type TTR protein can also pathologically accumulate in the heart, causing progressive cardiomyopathy in aging males, a condition named senile wild-type ATTR amyloidosis. Despite major advances in its diagnosis and treatment, the factors impacting the disease onset of hATTR amyloidosis and the risk of developing wtATTR amyloidosis are still largely unknown.
The primary objective of this study is to identify at genome-wide level (GWA) loci harboring
genetic variations that modify disease phenotype and severity modifiers of onset and risk of hATTR and wtATTR amyloidosis.

projects.title: Assessment of Selection Bias in MRI Analyses: A Study of Missing Modalities in MRI Protocols
projects.summary:
This research investigates potential biases in neuroimaging data collection within the "Insight 46" study, a longitudinal investigation of brain aging and Alzheimer's disease risk factors. Using magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), we will examine whether image quality and protocol completion rates systematically differ across participant characteristics such as health status, demographics, and cognitive function.

The project leverages the rich "Insight 46" dataset, which includes comprehensive longitudinal data from birth to age 69 across multiple health domains. By identifying and quantifying potential acquisition biases, we aim to improve the reliability of neuroimaging findings and ensure that research conclusions accurately represent the entire study population.

Our analyses will help determine if technical challenges in neuroimaging disproportionately affect certain participant groups, potentially leading to selection bias in studies of neurodegenerative diseases. This work addresses an important methodological concern in population-based neuroimaging research.

projects.title: Relationships between white matter hyperintensity volume and volume change with later cognitive decline
projects.summary: The aim of this study is to determine if damage to the white matter of the brain, responsible for communication and signalling between different brain areas, is related to later change in cognitive functions such as memory, attention and information processing

projects.title: Artificial Intelligence Applied to MRI of Dementia
projects.summary:
The student will pursue machine learning strategies to develop decision support tools that will integrate this multimodality information for use by neuroradiologists and neurologists, working with an established multidisciplinary group of researchers at the Centre for Medical Image Computing and the DRC, UCL. Tools to enable categorisation of disease at different granularities will be investigated, including, where appropriate, the identification and prediction of treatment side-effects.
The target output of the work will be tools to predict: the presence of AD in diagnosed individuals; the individualised likelihood for a non-symptomatic person in the cohort that they will develop AD; the time from the date of scan to the onset of AD symptoms.

projects.title: Associations between cardiac structure and function and blood pressure decline over the adult life course
projects.summary: As people grow older, their blood pressure often decreases—but the reasons behind this drop are not fully understood. Recent research suggests that subtle, early changes in how the heart is shaped and how it works might be responsible. This project will explore how age-related changes in the heart could lead to lower blood pressure, even before obvious heart disease appears. By improving our understanding of this connection, the research may help doctors better identify older adults who are at risk of heart problems and improve how we manage cardiovascular health in aging populations.

projects.title: Multimodal Analysis of Actigraphy and Cognitive Measures for Predicting Neurodegenerative Biomarkers
projects.summary: This project aims to improve our understanding of how sleep patterns, circadian rhythms, and cognitive abilities relate to brain health in older age. We will analyse actigraphy data (e.g., total sleep time, sleep start and end times) obtained from wearable activity monitors, and cognitive abilities (e.g., memory, reaction times, problem-solving) measured using online computerised tests. By examining how these measurements relate to each other, and whether combining them provides a more accurate prediction of neurodegenerative disease biomarkers (e.g., brain scans, blood tests), we aim to shed light on more precise and sensitive ways of detecting the early signs of neurodegenerative disease.

projects.title: Predicting mental health, physical health, and functional outcomes across the lifespan using a polygenic score for transdiagnostic neurodevelopmental traits.
projects.summary: Neurodevelopmental conditions such as autism, ADHD, and learning difficulties frequently co-occur, share underlying genetic factors, and are associated with a range of negative long-term outcomes. This project will investigate whether an aggregate measure of genetic liability shared across neurodevelopmental conditions (captured by a polygenic score) predicts outcomes across the life-course. Specifically, using data from two UK cohort studies, the Millennium Cohort Study and the National Survey of Health and Development, we will investigate the association between polygenic scores and measures of mental and physical health, cognitive performance, lifestyle behaviours, and educational, occupational, and social outcomes across childhood, adolescence and adulthood time points. The findings may promote early identification and support strategies to prevent long-term outcomes in individuals with neurodevelopmental conditions.

projects.title: The relationship between dietary folate and depression symptoms at certain points in the life course - an observational retrospective longitudinal study design using participants from the UK National Survey for Health and Development
projects.summary: This study explores whether low intake of dietary folate—a B-vitamin found in foods like legumes, cereals, and eggs, measured from diet diaries—is linked to symptoms of depression at different stages of life. It uses data from the National Survey of Health and Development, a long-running UK study that has followed people born in 1946 for over 75 years. Researchers will examine folate intake from as earlier as age 4 and look at depression symptoms reported in later ages to examine if the two are related. The study uses a statistical method called marginal structural modelling, which helps to better understand cause-and-effect relationships in long-term studies. This approach is useful because it can account for changes in health and lifestyle over time. The findings could help inform if dietary folate is related to depression symptoms and whether improving folate intake might reduce the risk of depression in life.

projects.title: FnIRs to Elucidate Brain-heart InTeractions (FIREBIT)
projects.summary: Cardiovascular disease is a major risk factor for cognitive impairment and dementia. Functional near infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) is a non-invasive technique that measures changes in tissue oxygenation in the brain. Its portability enables assessments both at rest and during exercise, enabling dynamic assessment of brain function. However, developments in signal processing techniques and analysis pipelines are required to advance fNIRS to a widespread tool for the assessment of brain and cardiovascular function.

projects.title: Electromagnetic Tissue Properties in Healthy Ageing and Dementia: A Longitudinal Study Using QSM and EPT
projects.summary:
This project will explore how the brain’s electromagnetic tissue properties change with age in the early stages of Alzheimer’s disease. Using advanced magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) techniques, we will measure two key features: magnetic susceptibility, which is linked to iron and myelin content, and electrical conductivity, which reflects ionic composition. Both of these properties may change before symptoms appear, providing new insights into the pathological processes that lead to dementia.

Using MRI data from the British 1946 Birth Cohort (Insight 46), we will perform quantitative mapping of both susceptibility and conductivity, and investigate changes with age and in relation to amyloid-β PET status, cognitive performance, and other relevant clinical variables. Ultimately, we aim to determine whether these novel MRI measures can improve earlier detection and monitoring of Alzheimer’s disease.

projects.title: Generational changes in diet quality (quantified by a Mediterranean diet score), their association blood pressure, and the role of socioeconomic inequalities
projects.summary:
We are investigating how changes in people’s diet over generations affects blood pressure in mid-life. In particular, we want to understand whether eating in greater accordance with the Mediterranean diet is linked to lower blood pressure levels, an important indicator of overall health, especially cardiovascular health. We will also look at whether differences in diet between socioeconomic groups help to explain why blood pressure is higher in some people than others. 

We will use data from two large, long-term studies that have followed people born in Britain in 1946 and 1970. By comparing these two generations, we can see how diet and blood pressure patterns have changed over time, and whether inequalities are narrowing or widening. Overall, this research will contribute to understanding how lifestyle and social factors affect health across generations, and how we might aim to reduce inequalities in health markers such as high blood pressure in the future.

projects.title: The stress and rest perfusion phenotypes of older age participants in the MyoFit46 study
projects.summary: MyoFit46 is the cardiovascular substudy of the NSHD and it undertook stress perfusion CMR in 500 older age participants. The student will analyse the stress and rest perfusion data of participants and report on the observed phenotypes including discoveries of inducible ischaemia and how these correlate with foci of LGE.
