projects.title: The electrocardiographic imaging phenotypes of older age participants in the MyoFit46 Study
projects.summary:
The project is a cardiovascular study undertaking CMR with
electrocardiographic imaging (ECGI) in 500 older age participants. The processed ECGI data of participants will be analysed, reporting on the observed phenotypes
including discoveries of LV activation time dispersion, heterogeneity and fractionation.

projects.title: Normal reference ranges of electrocardiographic imaging parameters of the older age heart
projects.summary:
Ageing alters the hearts electrical behaviour, yet ECGI specific normal values in order adults remain limited. By leveraging existing MyoFit46 ECGI data we aim to develop normal ref ranges for the older age heart. Using daat captured via capturECGI vest in conjunction with cardiac magnetic resonance. (CMR), we will characterise typical, non invasive electrical patterns in adults aged ≥60 years. Results will be summarised at whole heart and standard regional levels and will be stratified by age (and possibly sex). 
Our aim is to deliver concise, publication reference ranges for key ECGI measures in elderly life that are suitable for clinical interpretation and research benchmarking. Establishment of these normal ranges will help lay the groundwork for future ECGI work in looking at arrhythmia risk and sudden cardiac death stratification; supporting more personalised decision making in older adults.

projects.title: Neurocardiac amyloid across cohorts: multimodal discovery in Insight46/MyoFit46 with replication and validation in UK Biobank
projects.summary: Increasing evidence has suggested that amyloid-β, a protein associated with Alzheimer's, may also affect heart health and function, posing a large threat to the health of the wider population. However, the distinct set of heart-related features linked to Alzheimer’s, and particularly to the presence of amyloid-β in the heart, is yet to be identified. Therefore, this study aims to better understand this connection between the heart and brain. We will plan to use large cohorts of data to assess the heart function of those found with amyloid-β in their brains, compared to those with vascular problems in the brain, those only with reduced heart function and healthy individuals. We will also look at blood protein data to identify any patterns related to heart health and ageing, and later we plan to test our findings in a larger national dataset to see if our results hold true across different ages and health risks. Through this work, we hope to better understand heart health in early Alzheimer’s disease, to create opportunities for earlier diagnosis, better prevention and improved care for millions at risk of these heart and brain conditions.

projects.title: Historical trends in brain volumes and brain ageing
projects.summary:
In a new research project, we intend to investigate whether historic trends of falling age-adjusted dementia incidence rates are mirrored by secular improvements in age-adjusted measures of brain structure across generations. Moreover, we want to investigate whether potential intergenerational differences are more compatible with the brain reserve or with the brain maintenance hypothesis of healthy ageing.
To this end, we aim to draw on a large number of neuroimaging studies to cover a broad range of ages and years of birth and to answer our research questions as precisely and robustly as possible.
projects.institution: Max Planck Institute for Human Cognitive and Brain Sciences

projects.title: The electrocardiographic imaging phenotypes of older age participants in the MyoFit46 Study
projects.summary:
MyoFit46 is the cardiovascular substudy of the NSHD and it undertook CMR with
electrocardiographic imaging (ECGI) in 500 older age participants. We will analyse
the already processed ECGI data of participants and report on the observed phenotypes
including discoveries of LV activation time dispersion, heterogeneity and fractionation.

projects.title: Lifetime menstrual exposure and women’s pelvic health: Associations with endometriosis, fibroids, ovarian cysts and IBS in a prospective cohort
projects.summary: This project explores how women’s reproductive histories influence the development of conditions such as endometriosis, uterine fibroids, ovarian cysts and irritable bowel syndrome (IBS). Modern reproductive patterns - earlier menarche (age at first menstrual cycle), fewer births, reduced breastfeeding and hormonal contraceptive use - mean women experience more menstrual cycles than in our ancestral past, potentially increasing exposure to hormonal and inflammatory processes linked to these conditions. Using the NSHD 1946 Birth Cohort, the study will test whether these reproductive factors predict later-life diagnoses and whether contraceptives show a distinct pattern of association. It will also examine whether IBS shares similar reproductive or inflammatory links. The findings aim to clarify how contemporary reproductive behaviours shape women’s midlife health in line with evolutionary mismatch theory, and identify which associations are strongest.

projects.title: Predictors of memory maintenance
projects.summary: We will use llongitudinal memory examinations to separate real memory stability from effects of test repetition and natural noise in memory scores. We will then investigate whether people who maintain memory also show signs of better brain health, and how their life history, health, and psychosocial factors differ from others. By clarifying how often genuine memory maintenance occurs, and what seems to support it, the project will improve our understanding of resilience in cognitive aging and may help inform strategies to protect memory in older age.

projects.title: Relationships between Subjective Cognitive Complaints, Amyloid Status, and Mental Health Outcomes Overtime: Comparisons Across Time in later life
projects.summary: Formal cognitive testing is used to detect objective changes in thinking related to Alzheimer’s disease (AD) and plays a key role in diagnosis. A subset of individuals experience subjective cognitive decline (SCD), whereby they perform well on cognitive tests but report noticing changes in their thinking in everyday life. SCD has been shown to be a risk factor for developing dementia and has been related to preclinical changes in biomarkers for AD as well as mental health outcomes in prior studies. This project aims to build upon previous research conducted with individuals from the Insight 46 sub-study at age 70, by comparing relationships in SCD, amyloid status, objective cognitive performance, and mental health outcomes over time at ages 73 and 77. We hope this work will add to our understanding of SCD as a risk factor for AD in both clinical practice and research.

projects.title: UKLLC NSHD Data Deposits
projects.summary: To promote the data collected from the NSHD, we will be depositing data to the UKLLC TRE. This will allow researchers to be able to analyse the data securely and have the ability to merge these datasets with linkage data available via the UKLLC.

projects.title: Childhood IQ and CVRF
projects.summary: This study looks at whether childhood cognitive ability is linked to body weight in adolescence and early adulthood, and whether education helps explain this relationship. Understanding these pathways may provide insight into how early life experiences influence health later in life.

projects.title: External validation of biomarker-derived anaemia phenogroups and their associations with mortality and hospitalisation in NSHD
projects.summary: This project will look at whether anaemia can be grouped into a few meaningful “types” using routine blood test results, rather than relying only on a single haemoglobin cut-off. Using a large UK study, we previously found that people with anaemia often fall into distinct patterns that seem to reflect different underlying health problems, and these patterns were linked to very different risks of death and hospital admission over both the short and long term. We now want to repeat and confirm these findings in the NSHD study as an independent UK population, to check whether the same patterns appear and whether they predict outcomes in a similar way. If confirmed, this could help doctors understand anaemia better, identify higher-risk patients earlier, and guide more appropriate follow-up and assessment using information that is already commonly collected in clinical care.

projects.title: Structural and functional Carotid ageing and cognitive function in Insight46 (under revision)
projects.summary: This project aims to examine whether the thickening and stiffness of the carotid artery is associated with cognitive decline in older adults from Insight46, the neurological-sub study of the MRC National Survey of Health and Development. Using longitudinal vascular and cognitive data from Phases 2 and 3 of the research study, we will evaluate the relationship with changes in cognitive performance over time. To account for potential confounding and life-course influences, additional NSHD covariates will be required, including BMI, smoking history, socio-economic status, education level, childhood cognition, age and sex will be incorporated from earlier waves of the cohort prior to Insight46. The proposed output is a concise analytical report summarising the findings, including tables, figures and interpretation relevant to vascular ageing and dementia risk within this well-characterised birth cohort.

projects.title: Secondary education and social change in the United Kingdom since 1945
projects.summary: A project exploring the experience of secondary education in the UK since 1945 from the perspective of pupils, parents, and communities.

projects.title: Is the AD8 a valid and potentially superior tool to the CDR for remote, scalable assessment of early clinical change in preclinical Alzheimer’s disease?
projects.summary:
The Alzheimer’s Disease 8-item questionnaire (AD8) is a short set of questions completed by someone who knows the participant well, such as a family member or friend. It asks about changes in memory and thinking and may be useful for identifying early cognitive change, particularly when in-person assessments are not possible. 

This project will use data from the Insight 46 study to examine how AD8 scores change over time and how they relate to performance on cognitive tests and to brain scan measures linked to Alzheimer’s disease. By comparing the AD8 with the Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) scale, a more detailed clinical assessment, this work aims to understand whether the AD8 could be a useful tool for identifying early cognitive change in the preclinical stages of Alzheimer’s disease.

projects.title: Persistence of healthy weight across cohorts
projects.summary:
Studies that follow people over many years show that people born more recently in Britain are more likely to be overweight or obese than people from older generations when they reach the same age. However, we still know less about how many people manage to stay at a healthy weight throughout their lives, and how this has changed from one generation to the next.

In this project, we will use information from three large British cohort studies that have followed people born in 1946, 1958 and 1970 from birth into adulthood. By looking at measurements of height and weight collected at different ages, we will estimate how many people have always stayed at a healthy weight, how many have been overweight at some point in their lives, and how many have ever had obesity. 

Understanding these patterns will help us see how the risk of overweight and obesity has changed across generations. It will also help us estimate how many people in the population might benefit from support to lose weight in the future, including new treatments such as weight-loss medicines. This information can help health services plan for the types of care people may need.

projects.title: Developing Process Metrics for the Complex Figure Drawing Test in pre-clinical Alzheimer’s disease
projects.summary: The Complex Figure Drawing Test has been shown to capture early cognitive changes which associate the deteriorating brain in Alzheimer’s dementia before symptoms and diagnosis. In the latest phase of the Insight 46 study, participants have used digital pens to draw these complex figures from memory immediately and following a delay. Using the digital pen, we can generate a host of information on task performance, which might be subtly different in those with early cognitive impairment, including decision making (think time vs ink time), speed, efficiency and precision measures. We aim to determine how such measures compare to brain health – comparing them with brain scans, blood tests and Alzheimer’s disease-related markers. This might help us understand and test for very early changes in Alzheimer’s disease before clinical manifestation or diagnosis.

projects.title: Cardiovascular incidental findings in Insight46 Phase 3
projects.summary: I have been given permission to use this data. I currently do all the analysis and incidental findings for the cardiovascular tests which I am writing about.

projects.title: Predicting Late-Life Cognitive Impairment in the 1946 British Birth Cohort
projects.summary:
Dementia is a major global health challenge, but it is often diagnosed too late; by the time clinical symptoms appear, significant brain damage has already occurred. This project aims to determine if individuals at high risk of memory problems can be identified much earlier by evaluating their health across their entire life.

Using data from the 1946 British Birth Cohort, a risk prediction model will be built based on early-life factors (such as childhood education), mid-life health (such as blood pressure, BMI, and hearing loss), and late-life wellbeing. Traditional statistical methods will be used to predict cognitive impairment at age 77. The project also aims to test if Machine Learning can predict these memory problems more accurately than traditional statistics. By identifying the most effective way to predict cognitive decline using lifelong data, this research could eventually help doctors intervene earlier.
projects.institution: London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine

projects.title: Autobiographical selfhood in Britain, c.1950-2008/9
projects.summary: This project asks how and why did people become ‘authors of their own lives’ in the second half of the twentieth century? How far did different individuals construct themselves as reflexive agents, making their own choices and fortunes? Analysing differences of race, gender, class and place, this project considers how far the rise of autobiographical selfhood, a story often told in universal terms, was more partial. Such an approach lets us see the drivers of this change more clearly, revealing how it affected different kinds of people at different moments. Where much attention has been devoted to autobiography as a genre, I focus on the vast majority of Britons who did not write, let alone publish, an autobiography. I use archived social-science material, as well as qualitative longitudinal birth cohort data, to reconstruct the stories that ‘ordinary’ men and women told about their lives as they were living them. These questions hold contemporary significance. In an age when our ways of thinking about the self are changing again, as social media impacts our self-image, there are clear payoffs to returning to this earlier historical juncture, asking where did this particular way of thinking come from? Where did it go?

projects.title: A book project about the survey history and study members, focusing on education
projects.summary: A history book about the 1946 cohort, focusing on the educational journeys of the study members, and the educational findings of the scientists.

projects.title: Validation of plasma biomarkers for aging and neurodegeneration in Asian Indian populations
projects.summary:
The long-term goal of CBR is to enable ‘healthy aging’ through significant contribution to minimising the burden of neurodegenerative diseases. CBR is presently working on developing a composite biomarker for early detection of dementia and design scalable interventions to prevent/postpone dementia. Towards this, the Centre integrates expertise in neuroscience, clinical research, genomics, data science, and engineering to advance early diagnosis, prevention, and intervention strategies. CBR’s large-scale cohort studies, multidisciplinary research, and commitment to innovative partnerships place it at the forefront of aging brain research in India.

CBR has embarked on setting up a Biomarker Centre of Excellence in collaboration with the UK Dementia Research Institute (UK DRI) and with support from Gates Ventures. This ambitious initiative aims to establish a sophisticated platform for the discovery and validation of neurodegenerative disease biomarkers. In addition to plasma biomarkers, the Centre will also explore digital biomarkers to build a more comprehensive understanding of disease onset and progression.

A unique strength of this Centre of Excellence is that it will function under the scientific guidance of Professor Henrik Zetterberg (UK DRI and University of Gothenburg), a globally recognised pioneer in biomarker research, and Professor Siddharthan Chandran, Director of the UK DRI, both of whom are Visiting Faculty Members at CBR. By working closely with Professors Zetterberg and Chandran, the Centre will integrate the state-of-the-art in fluid biomarker assays, high-throughput proteomics, and AI-driven analytics with unique, diverse cohorts from India and the UK in order to accelerate breakthroughs in early diagnosis. The Centre of Excellence will foster cross-institutional partnerships, training, and knowledge exchange to build capacity and advance global brain health research.
projects.institution: Center for Brain Research, Indian Institute of Science

projects.title: Development of a Vision-Independent ACE-III for Cognitive Screening
projects.summary: Despite the considerable overlap between ageing, dementia, and visual impairment, widely used cognitive screening tools such as the Addenbrooke’s Cognitive Examination III (ACE-III) are not well suited for individuals with significant visual impairment. Many subtests rely heavily on visual processing and individuals with substantial sight loss may be at increased risk of misclassification. The primary aim of this analysis is to investigate the relationship between total ACE-III scores and performance on vision-dependent items. This will allow us to quantify the extent to which visual demands influence overall scores and to assess whether visual impairment could bias cognitive classification. Understanding this relationship is essential for improving the interpretation of ACE-III scores in populations with visual impairment and will provide an empirical foundation for the development of more accessible and equitable cognitive screening tools.

projects.title: Developing a sex-specific PROSPR Intrinsic Capacity score using the MRC National Survey of Health and Development (NSHD)
projects.summary: As people age, they experience a decline in intrinsic capacity (IC) – the combined physical and mental abilities that support independence and health. The World Health Organization recognizes IC as a key measure of aging, but there are no affordable, validated tests to track it. Current approaches are either disease-focused or restricted to costly private health programs, and clinical trials remain long and slow because there is no reliable proxy for aging-related decline. We propose to create a refined IC score: a practical, science-based way to estimate resilience and predict long-term outcomes such as mortality, multimorbidity, functional ability and hospitalization. The score will integrate information from health surveys, functional assessments, wearable devices, and blood-based biomarkers, pooled from multiple large longitudinal datasets including NSHD, to provide the most accurate prediction of health trajectory.

projects.title: Mental health trajectories and epigenetic ageing
projects.summary:
Depression, anxiety, and other emotional difficulties are increasingly recognised as important factors that may influence brain health and dementia risk. However, little is known about whether mental health problems at different stages of life, from childhood through to adulthood, have lasting effects on how we age.

This project will use data from the National Survey of Health and Development (NSHD), the world's longest-running birth cohort study, which has followed the same individuals from birth into older age. The study will examine how patterns of affective symptoms across the life course are associated with important markers of ageing, telomere length, epigenetic ageing clocks, and MRI-derived brain age.

By investigating whether the timing, persistence, and accumulation of affective symptoms are linked to these markers, the research will improve understanding of how mental health may influence the biological processes associated with ageing and dementia risk. The project will also explore whether these relationships differ between men and women and across socioeconomic groups. Findings could help identify critical periods for intervention and inform strategies to promote healthier cognitive ageing throughout life.

projects.title: Birthday Banners
projects.summary: We are compiling facts and figures to showcase on the 80th birthday banners

projects.title: Assessment of genome-wide and polygenic association with schizotypy across multiple cohorts.
projects.summary: Schizotypy or sub-clinical experiences of psychosis are constructs that encompasses a set of personality traits bearing a resemblance to the clinical manifestation of schizophrenia. This association is thought to be underpinned by common underlying genetics, as higher levels of schizotypy-like experiences are most frequently found in individuals with a family history of schizophrenia. However, unlike schizophrenia, studies of schizotypy-like experiences are not systematically confounded by the influences of active psychosis or anti-psychotic medication. Therefore, it may be an important intermediate phenotype as provides a framework for investigating the etiology and pathophysiology of schizophrenia spectrum disorders and thus improve understanding surrounding the genetic, environmental and psychological architecture. We sought to understand the genomics of schizotypy-like experiences using multiple cohorts, and performing a harmonization step across studies to combine questionnaire features to perform a meta analysis to increase statistical power.

projects.title: Multi-cohort meta-analysis of impulsivity and risk-taking
projects.summary: As both impulsivity and risk-taking are heritable, studying the genetic aetiology of these endophenotypes may give insights into the genomic basis of mental illness. We have conducted a genome-wide association study (GWAS) of impulsivity in the Generation Scotland (GS) cohort (N=854). Polygenic associations were investigated using summary statistics derived from independent GWAS on associated phenotypes. In the modest-sized GS cohort, we report a GWAS-significant association between rs6820980 and impulsivity (p=2.25×10-8). Polygenic profile scores showed significant positive associations with ADHD (p-value = 1.30×10-5), conscientiousness (p-value = 0.0024) and educational attainment (p-value = 0.00026) with impulsivity. We plan to perform a meta-analysis of impulsivity and risk taking including additional CLS cohorts, undertaking the same types of analysis in these independent cohorts, including risk-taking from UK Biobank. We will test the overlap and independence of the polygenic signal between risk-taking and impulsivity, as well as the genetic correlation between the two.

projects.title: Social asymmetry and morbidity across countries
projects.summary: While it is widely recognized that social isolation and loneliness negatively impact health, these two experiences do not always align. The discrepancy between an individual's objective lack of social connections and their subjective feelings of loneliness is known as "social asymmetry". Recent evidence indicates that older adults experiencing "social vulnerability"—those who feel significantly lonelier than expected given their actual levels of social contact—face a substantially increased risk of incident cardiovascular disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and all-cause mortality. However, this foundational research relies almost exclusively on data from a high-income, predominantly White population in England. Our proposed multi-country cohort project seeks to expand this framework globally by analyzing longitudinal data across both high-income and low-income nations. We will investigate whether the severe health risks associated with a mismatch between subjective loneliness and objective isolation are a universal human trait or are significantly shaped by diverse macroeconomic and cultural environments. Ultimately, understanding these distinct patterns of social experience will help international policymakers and healthcare providers design targeted interventions to support socially vulnerable older adults and promote healthy aging worldwide.

projects.title: HPA axis candidate genes, early life adversity, and cortisol in late life
projects.summary:
This project aims to improve understanding of how genes and early life experiences shape the body’s stress response. Specifically, it focuses on the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal (HPA) axis, which controls the release of the stress hormone cortisol.

Using NSHD data, we will examine whether certain genetic differences interact with early life adversity—such as childhood stress or hardship—to influence cortisol levels in older adults. We will also build on an existing genetic scoring method that combines information from multiple genes to better predict stress system functioning.

By clarifying how genetic and environmental factors interact throughout life, this research may help improve our understanding of stress-related conditions such as depression and post-traumatic stress disorder. In the long run, it could contribute to better prevention strategies and more personalized approaches to treatment.

projects.title: Multi-cohort meta-analysis of the genomics of perceived and observed social support
projects.summary: Genes play an important role in shaping social behaviour as they modulate brain activity through molecular pathways; therefore, it can be said that genes regulate the expression of behaviour. Social support is correlated with an individual’s mental health as these social interactions require effective communication and participation. It may be that how someone perceives their social support or how frequently they participate in social support have different levels of genetic control and/or have different genetic pathways. We would like to use information from these cohorts to perform a genetic analysis of social support by studying differences in the DNA of individuals, harmonise these data with data from different cohorts and perform an overall study combining the individual study results.

projects.title: PEpi Score: Polygenic Epistatic Scoring
projects.summary: Human genetic studies generally examine the association between the outcome and (a) single genetic markers and (b) an additive collection of multiple genetic markers. However, epistasis, or gene-gene interactions, are commonly found in mammalian animal models, and they can explain a sizeable proportion of the variation in complex traits. This study seeks to develop a novel statistical method that models the additive portion plus the epistatic component of several human traits.

projects.title: How does high blood pressure affect the risk of dementia?
projects.summary: High blood pressure is a common condition that affects millions of people worldwide and is thought to increase the risk of dementia. However, it is not yet fully understood how blood pressure across different stages of adult life influences cognitive health in later life. This study will use information from the Medical Research Council National Survey of Health and Development (NSHD), also known as the 1946 British Birth Cohort, to investigate the relationship between blood pressure and later-life cognitive impairment and dementia. The research will examine whether maintaining healthy blood pressure throughout adulthood, and receiving treatment for high blood pressure, is associated with better cognitive health in older age. The findings may help improve understanding of dementia prevention and support public health strategies aimed at promoting healthy ageing.
projects.institution: London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine

projects.title: Identifying putative novel causal pathways emerging in the first decades of life which may increase risk of poor heart and brain health in later-life
projects.summary: Cardiovascular disease and dementia share many risk factors, yet it remains unclear how early in the lifecourse these begin to exert their impact and through which biological pathways. Part of the difficulty of linking early-life risk factors to later-life outcomes is the long period of time between them, meaning that many studies of young people have information on exposures but no outcomes while conversely studies of older people have outcomes but not information on exposures in early-life. This study aims to get around these issues by stratifying young people by their known genetic liability for future disease and then attempting to establish how their risk factors differ as they move throuugh childhood to midlife.

projects.title: Neurodiversity symptoms in childhood in relation to adult physical and mental health:  Examining the explanatory role of IQ, mental distress, and socioeconomic status in the UK 1946 birth cohort
projects.summary: While neurodevelopmental conditions such as Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD)  are increasingly recognised,  there is a gap in our understanding of if and how these conditions impact mental and physical health in older adulthood. We will utilise the British birth cohorts 1946, 1958, and 1970 to examine these correlations.

projects.title: Data-driven characterization of spatiotemporal amyloid deposition patterns in early Alzheimer’s disease
projects.summary: This project aims to investigate differential patterns of spatiotemporal amyloid-beta (Aβ) deposition in early Alzheimer’s disease, using  Aβ-PET scans from multiple cohorts and advanced deep representation learning models to characterize heterogeneity in Aβ distribution. This approach seeks to identify patterns of Aβ burden that deviate from the typical trajectory of amyloid accumulation, and which may provide critical insight into dissociable pathways of disease progression. We will further validate the identified data-driven patterns through comparison with regional assessments at baseline, as well as longitudinally using follow-up Aβ-PET, to evaluate their stability and clinical relevance over time. In addition, we will assess the association of the identified patterns with clinical outcomes (e.g., cognition, progression to dementia) and baseline biomarkers (e.g., CSF, genetics, MRI) to determine their prognostic value and biological significance.

projects.title: Early life health origins of family outcomes: A longitudinal analysis of adolescent health and partnership and fertility trajectories
projects.summary:
Many high-income societies, including the UK, are experiencing trends of delayed parenthood and declining fertility.

These trends have been partly linked to educational expansion, shifting values toward greater personal freedom, and, more recently, economic uncertainty. However, these factors do not fully account for the significant changes in family behaviours across generations. One less widely explored determinant is early-life health, which may play a fundamental role.

This project aims to address this gap by investigating how early-life health shapes partnership and fertility trajectories across cohorts and life stages, using longitudinal data from five British cohort studies:

1946 National Survey for Health and Development (NSHD) ; 1958 National Child Development Study (NCDS); 1970 British Cohort Study (BCS70); Next Steps; and UK Household Longitudinal Study.

This project will address the following questions:

1) What is the association between early-life health and later-life partnership and fertility trajectories among cohorts who have completed their childbearing years? How has it changed across cohorts?
2) What is the association between early-life health and first partnership formation and transition to parenthood? How has it changed across cohorts?
3) What is the association between early-life health and expectations for family transitions among cohorts who are currently in their active childbearing years?

projects.title: MMSE sentence analysis in pre-clinical Alzheimer’s disease
projects.summary: Analysis of spontaneous language could reveal more information about cognition and mood than traditional neuropsychological tests, while being less onerous for test participants. We propose to analyse de-identified sentences written by participants of the Insight46 cohort as part of the Mini-Mental State Examination. To assess the clinical usefulness of sentence analysis, we will compare its results with standardised measures of cognition and mood from the same participants. We will also investigate whether sentence analysis could be useful for identifying individuals in the very early stages of dementia by comparisons with established disease biomarkers.

projects.title: Using MRI to identify Alzheimer's-specific Pathology: A Non-invasive CompanionDiagnostic to Amyloid Disease-Modifying Treatments
projects.summary: We aim to enable more precise and specific diagnosis of Alzheimer’s disease (AD) by combining MRI brain scanning with new computer technology. MRI brain scans are a routine part of the assessment of patients with memory problems, but when interpreted by humans are unable to detect subtle changes and cannot identify AD-specific proteins. We have developed and aim to test a technology that applies advanced computerised processing to MRI scans to determine whether abnormal AD proteins are present. We will apply the technology in scans acquired from participants in the Insight-46 project to assess how well it identifies early protein build-up

projects.title: Heart and Brain - Arrhythmia project
projects.summary:
Sudden cardiac death and dangerous heart rhythms, known as arrhythmias, remain a major health challenge. One important factor in these conditions is the autonomic nervous system — the part of our nervous system that automatically controls functions such as heart rate and blood pressure. Importantly, the heart and brain are constantly communicating with each other. The brain can influence how the heart behaves through the autonomic nervous system, while signals from the heart can also travel back to the brain and affect how the nervous system responds.
Our research aims to better understand this two-way communication between the heart and the brain using modern techniques to map the activity. We will study how these signals interact and how they may contribute to abnormal heart rhythms. The first stage of the project will focus on discovering and understanding these heart–brain connections. What we learn will then help us develop more personalised treatments for people with different types of arrhythmias. In the second stage, we will investigate a non-invasive approach called tragus nerve stimulation. This involves gently stimulating a nerve through the ear to influence the autonomic nervous system. We will use the heart–brain mapping techniques developed in the first stage to understand how this treatment works and, importantly, which patients are most likely to benefit. Ultimately, our goal is to improve our understanding of how the brain and heart work together and use that knowledge to develop safer, more targeted treatments for dangerous heart rhythms and to reduce the risk of sudden cardiac death.

projects.title: Insight into plasma p-tau217 as a new blood-based biomarker
projects.summary: It has become increasingly more important to quickly and accurately identify Alzheimer's disease (AD) in the early stages, for potential treatment. Recent studies have shown the potential of blood-based biomarkers as a good diagnostic tool for pre-screening, due to their non-invasive nature and high accuracy in distinguishing individuals with and without amyloid-beta pathology. Especially, plasma p-tau217 has shown great potential for such a pre-screen tool. However, more research needs to be done with regards to prevalence in different clinical groups, and plasma level changes over time and with changing cognition.

projects.title: Has the mortality penalty of childhood socioeconomic disadvantage changed across British birth cohorts? A cross-cohort causal analysis of the 1946, 1958 and 1970 cohorts.
projects.summary: People born into poorer family circumstances tend to die younger, but it is unclear whether this gap has widened or narrowed for people born in different decades. This project compares three groups of British people - those born in 1946, 1958 and 1970 - who have each been followed since birth. For every group we measure how strongly a child's family social class predicts dying earlier in adult life, using modern causal-analysis methods that make the groups fairly comparable and account for factors present at birth such as the mother's age and the area of birth. Comparing the strength of this link across the three generations shows whether the survival disadvantage of a poorer start in life is getting bigger, smaller, or staying the same. The findings will help show whether social inequalities in early death have changed over time and inform efforts to reduce them.

projects.title: Changing health-mortality associations across three British birth cohorts
projects.summary:
Britain has some of the longest running birth cohort studies in the world, following different generations of people from birth through to old age. These birth cohort studies show something concerning: people born more recently are more likely to be living with obesity, poor mental health, a other long-term health conditions than people born decades earlier were at the same age. We have called this pattern a "generational health drift".

At the same time, official projections suggest that people are still expected to live longer than previous generations, on average. This raises a puzzle. If younger generations are experiencing worse health earlier in life, will they still end up living longer, as predicted? Better medical treatment may mean that having a health condition no longer shortens life the way it one did. But there are also worrying signs that improvements in survival during midlife have been slowing in the UK, and one possible reason is that people are spending more of their lives living with poor health. 

This project will use data from the 1946 MRC National Survey of Health and Development, together with two other large birth cohort studies of people born in 1958 and 1970, to help answer this question. We will first check how death rates in these studies compare with official national records. We will then examine whether the relationship between common physical or mental health conditions early in life and dying prematurely has changed across generations, focusing especially on obesity and mental ill-health. The findings will help us understand whether today's health trends are likely to affect longevity, with implications for policies on disease prevention and planning for furture health and social care needs as the population ages.
